sentences.text: The only valid species is Valdosaurus canaliculatus, originally based on juvenile femurs that would have grown into medium-sized euornithopods with legs reaching half a meter in length.
In life, the newly described specimen would have measured around 4 to 5 meters in length.

Rev. William Fox collected two small femora near Cowleaze Chine on the Isle of Wight in the 19th century. In 1889, Richard Lydekker assigned the remains to Camptosaurus valdensis based on a partial lower jaw and other bones, deriving the name from the Old English word 'weald'. In 1975, Peter Galton assigned the femora to Dryosaurus canaliculatus after concluding they did not belong to Camptosaurus. The genus Valdosaurus was established by Peter Galton in 1977, and the species Valdosaurus canaliculatus was named by him in 1975.

Valdosaurus caudal vertebrae have lengthened, backswept neural spines that overhang more than one following vertebra, a trait distinct from other ornithischians. Unlike other dryosaurids, Valdosaurus canaliculatus has an open obturator notch on the pubis.

Sedimentological data suggests the depositional environment of the Wessex Formation was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits. Burned plant and insect material and fusain suggest that the environment experienced frequent wildfires.
Valdosaurus is generally classified as a member of the family Dryosauridae, though Peter Galton originally assigned it to the paraphyletic family Hypsilophodontidae.

Valdosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous, approximately between 130 and 125 million years ago in the Barremian stage. Valdosaurus lived in what is now Europe, with fossils found on the Isle of Wight and other parts of England. The rock units where Valdosaurus fossils were found were deposited between the Berriasian and Barremian, approximately 145 to 125 million years ago.

It is debated whether many English specimens, including cranial elements and teeth, truly belong to Valdosaurus. The presence of Valdosaurus in Spain remains questionable. It is uncertain whether many of the English specimens truly belong to Valdosaurus, including all cranial material and teeth.
